headline: Hoeru is from Proto-Japonic *pəyu, and cognate with Kunigami buirun.
Dō is first cited to 1604 in the Portuguese work Arte da Lingoa de Iapam.
Shinzō is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 臓 (zō, “internal organ”).
Kakuchō is 拡 (kaku, “expand”) plus 張 (chō, “stretch”).
Tsūyaku is from Sinitic 通譯 (tōngyì).
Kazan is Middle Chinese 火山, literally “flaming mountain”.
Wakare is the continuative stem of 別れる (wakareru, “to separate, to part ways, to bid farewell”).
Bu, “non-”, is from Middle Chinese 無, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Ku, “phrase”, is from Middle Chinese 句 (kjuᴴ, “phrase”).
Yattsukeru is a shift from 遣り付ける (yaritsukeru): yari plus 付ける (tsukeru, “perform an action vigorously”).
Shina is simply from Old Japanese.
Jōhō is a contraction of 情況報告 (jōkyō hōkoku, “situation report”).
Kochira is こち (kochi, “this direction (or person)”) plus 等 (-ra, suffix of rough indication or approximation).
Tēpurekōdā is borrowed from English tape recorder.
Tsūkin was coined after 通う (kayou, “to regularly visit”) and 勤め (tsutome), with the kanji shifted to on'yomi in the compound.
Tsukue, “desk”, is simply listed as inherited from Old Japanese.
Reigai is 例 (rei, “usual practice”) plus 外 (gai, “outside”): outside the usual practice.
Mā is onomatopoeic.
Omowazu is the negative continuative of 思う.
Zenzen is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 全然 (quánrán) in the early 1800s, at first with furigana reading it まったく (mattaku).
Chōmiryō is 調味 (chōmi, “seasoning”) plus 料 (-ryō, “material”).
Tsukeru is from Old Japanese 付く (tuku), following the lower bigrade conjugation.
Gendai is 現 (gen, “current, now”) plus 代 (dai, “age, period”).
Tsukkomu is 突く (tsuku, “to poke”) plus 込む (komu, “to put into”).
Hyōhon is Literary Chinese 標本 (biāoběn), “the uppermost branches and the root”.
Murasaki is possibly 群 (mura, “gathering, group”) plus 咲き (saki, “blooming”).
Jun, “order”, is from Middle Chinese 順 (MC zywinH).
Nasaru is 成す (nasu, “to do”) plus a classical る suffix, irregularly evolved to godan conjugation.
Kawaku, “to be thirsty”, is related to 乾く (kawaku, “dry”).
Kushi, “comb”, is cognate with 串 (kushi, “skewer”).
